enhanced.fullText:
The Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems (sUAS) regulation, codified under 14 CFR Part 107, governs the operation of commercial small unmanned aircraft by higher education institutions within the National Airspace System. This Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) rule, effective August 29, 2016, permits universities to operate drones weighing less than 55 pounds for research, educational, and academic purposes without traditional airworthiness certification requirements.

Under 14 CFR § 107.1, institutions must ensure all sUAS operations comply with specific operational limitations. The aircraft must weigh less than 55 pounds including payload, operate only during daylight hours or civil twilight with appropriate anti-collision lighting per 14 CFR § 107.29, maintain visual line-of-sight with the unmanned aircraft throughout flight operations, and fly no higher than 400 feet above ground level in uncontrolled airspace.

Key personnel requirements under 14 CFR § 107.12 mandate that a certified remote pilot in command (RPIC) must hold a current remote pilot certificate issued under Part 107, be at least 16 years of age, and demonstrate aeronautical knowledge through FAA testing. Universities may allow uncertified individuals, including students and faculty, to manipulate flight controls provided they remain under direct supervision of a certified RPIC who maintains the ability to immediately assume control per 14 CFR § 107.19.

Institutional compliance obligations include aircraft registration under 49 U.S.C. § 44101 through the FAA's online system, with registration renewals required every three years. Operations over people require compliance with 14 CFR § 107.39 amendments effective April 21, 2021, establishing four categories of authorized flights based on aircraft weight and safety features.

Enforcement mechanisms under 49 U.S.C. § 46301 authorize civil penalties up to $27,500 per violation for individuals and $1,100,000 for institutions. The FAA may pursue certificate suspension, revocation, or criminal prosecution for willful violations. Recent regulatory updates include Remote ID requirements under 14 CFR § 107.57, mandating broadcast identification for most sUAS operations beginning September 16, 2023, and expanded night operations authorization under 14 CFR § 107.29 for properly equipped aircraft with certified RPICs completing recurrent training.
enhanced.summary: Federal regulation 14 CFR Part 107 permits higher education institutions to operate small unmanned aircraft systems under 55 pounds for research and educational purposes, requiring certified remote pilot supervision and compliance with operational limitations.
enhanced.requirements:
## Remote Pilot Certification Requirements
- Maintain certified remote pilot in command (RPIC) with current Part 107 certificate per 14 CFR § 107.12
- Ensure RPIC completes recurrent aeronautical knowledge testing every 24 months
- Document direct supervision when uncertified personnel operate controls per 14 CFR § 107.19

## Aircraft Registration and Compliance
- Register all sUAS weighing 0.55-55 pounds through FAA online system under 49 U.S.C. § 44101
- Renew aircraft registration every three years with current contact information
- Implement Remote ID compliance for operations after September 16, 2023 per 14 CFR § 107.57

## Operational Limitations
- Restrict flights to 400 feet AGL maximum altitude in uncontrolled airspace
- Maintain visual line-of-sight throughout all flight operations per 14 CFR § 107.31
- Operate only during daylight hours unless night operations waiver obtained
enhanced.reportingRequirements: Aircraft registration renewal required every three years through FAA online portal. Accident reporting mandatory within 10 days for incidents resulting in serious injury or property damage exceeding $500 per 14 CFR § 107.9.
